extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and educated readers of natural history/evolutionary biology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and assessing the criteria and types of evidence Darwin uses to argue for human descent, variation, and natural selection (comparative anatomy, embryology, population dynamics, and atavism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherited modifications from prolonged residence
rubrics_metrics.description: Residence during many generations at a great elevation tends, both directly and indirectly, to induce inherited modifications in the proportions of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: Mr. Forbes’s observations of high-plateau peoples carried down to low plains (higher mortality, surviving families show decreased characteristic peculiarities); measurements show differences in elongation and in lengths of femora/tibiae. Analogous modifications occur in domestic animals living in mountainous regions (Dr. Wilckens). Use multigenerational residence, direct observation, and explicit measurements to infer inherited change due to environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrested development (distinct from arrested growth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrested development: parts continue to grow whilst still retaining their early (embryonic) condition; differs from arrested growth where development halts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification: look for structures that retain early embryonic form despite further growth. Examples: cleft palate (occasionally inherited); microcephaly (skulls smaller, brain convolutions less complex, frontal sinus prominent, prognathous jaws), associated mental and behavioral traits (weak intelligence, inability to speak, imitation, quadrupedal climbing, hairiness). Use anatomical description, behavioral correlates, and inheritance reports (Vogt, Pinel, Maudsley) to classify cases as arrested development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversion (atavism) as evidence of descent
rubrics_metrics.description: When a structure arrested in development goes on growing so as to resemble a corresponding structure in a lower adult member of the same group, it may be considered a case of reversion (calling back a long-lost ancestral structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when anomalous adult structures match normal structures of lower taxa or the embryo of the taxon. Examples and evidence discussed: supernumerary mammae (including ectopic mammae and male rudimentary mammae), polydactylism (debated), duplicated or partially double uterus repeating lower mammal grades, division of malar and frontal bones persisting from fetal sutures, projecting canine teeth resembling apes, and development of muscles proper to Quadrumana. Consider counterarguments (alternative developmental explanations, rarity, or disputed homologies) and weigh frequency, symmetry, inheritance, anatomical correspondences, and comparative anatomy across taxa. Darwin notes some cases are doubtful and urges caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlated variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many structures are so intimately related that when one part varies another varies as well, often without an obvious causal explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize patterns of correlated change: homologous structures vary together (left/right sides, upper/lower extremities), muscles of the arm will often imitate those of the leg, and correlations occur among organs of sight and hearing, teeth and hair, and skin and hair colour/constitution. Use comparative and developmental data (Meckel, Geoffroy) to document associations; do not assume simple one-part causation—correlation may point to underlying developmental or constitutional factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneous variation
rubrics_metrics.description: A large class of variations appear to arise without any obvious external exciting cause and may be provisionally called spontaneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such variations as depending more on the organism’s constitution than on external conditions. Includes slight individual differences and abrupt deviations. Cross-reference with domestication studies (Variation under Domestication) for patterns and inheritance tendencies. Use cautious classification when causes are unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rate of increase and checks to population (Malthusian principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Populations possess substantial potential for rapid increase; the primary check to continued increase is difficulty of gaining subsistence and living in comfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify growth examples (civilised populations doubling in ~25 years; Euler’s calculation), and identify checks: restraint on marriage, higher infant mortality in poor classes, disease, epidemics, wars, emigration, famines, predators, infanticide and abortion, and social practices (licentiousness). Compare civilised vs savage fertility (domestication increasing fertility analogously), and use historical/case evidence (e.g., Santali increase after vaccination) to assess how checks operate in different societies and influence selection pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions required for natural selection to operate
rubrics_metrics.description: For natural selection to act there must be variability, exposure to a struggle for existence, and differential preservation of beneficial over injurious variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when a population is variable (in body or mind) and subject to diverse or changing conditions that impose a struggle for existence. Darwin emphasizes small individual differences (not only rare large deviations) as material for selection. Illustrative method: conceptually divide a population and show individuals better adapted (e.g., superior locomotory muscles) survive and procreate more. Use comparative anatomy, observed variability (e.g., muscular differences of hands/feet), and population-context reasoning to demonstrate selection’s action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key adaptive factors accounting for human dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Man’s supremacy is owed chiefly to intellectual faculties, social habits (mutual aid and defense), and corporeal structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the final evidential test of the 'battle for life' to weigh the relative importance of traits: intellect (including language—Darwin cites Chauncey Wright on the brain power required for language), invention and use of tools/weapons/rafts, and social cooperation. Document how these traits confer advantage in survival, dispersal, and competition with other species.
